Sorin Corina Cristea , 22.09.2026, 13:50 Following a two-hour meeting, the opposition Social Democratic Party, which holds the largest number of seats in the Romanian Parliament, announced it will vote against the government led by National Liberal MEP Siegfried Mureșan. PSD leader Sorin Grindeanu labeled the proposed cabinet “Bolojan 2.0”, pointing to the policies of former Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan. Dissatisfaction with those very policies led the Social Democrats to walk out of the ruling coalition with PNL, USR, and UDMR last spring, triggering the no-confidence motion that brought down the previous government. Grindeanu said that PSD will not support a cabinet that continues on Bolojan’s trajectory, though he noted a willingness to talk if Mureșan incorporates PSD’s 10-point plan into the government program: “If he wants to discuss with us, he needs to explain how he can incorporate into the government program the 10 recommendations we voted on in Sinaia. Since his nomination, I haven’t heard Mr. Mureșan mention these things or even indicate that he will consider PSD’s proposals. Our primary concern is policies that serve the Romanian people”. In a swift response on social media, the Prime Minister-designate argued that PSD has no interest in resolving the country’s political crisis, noting that the party rejected his cabinet before even reviewing its program or engaging in dialogue. Despite the opposition, Siegfried Mureșan remains determined to present his government program and cabinet list to Parliament, even without the 233 votes required for confirmation: “We will seek Parliament’s vote for several reasons. First, so the public knows what we are proposing for Romania—a modern state, a reformed central public administration, efficient local governance, and restructured state-owned enterprises. Second, to show citizens how every lawmaker and parliamentary group votes. And third, out of respect for Romania’s Constitution and the President; a nomination procedure must be treated with seriousness”. Mureșan is currently short by 64 votes, as the three parties supporting him hold just 169 seats combined. The task appears nearly impossible—especially as UDMR warned it will withdraw its support if confirmation relies on votes from extremist parties. Meanwhile, the Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR), which was excluded from coalition talks, reiterated that it will not vote for any government it is not a part of, insisting that early elections are the only way out of the current political stalemate. https://www.yorkpress.co.uk/news/nationa.text: Taoiseach confident of safety of Dublin summits despite hoax bomb threats By PA News Agency Share A Garda Armed Support Unit outside the entrance of the RTE headquarters in Dublin after staff at Ireland’s national broadcaster were evacuated following a bomb threat at its television and radio headquarters. Picture date: Friday November 6, 2026. This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. Irish premier Micheál Martin has expressed confidence that two major political summits being hosted in Dublin next week will pass off safely. Mr Martin’s comments came after several Irish media outlets received hoax bomb threats on Friday at the end of a week that saw airlines across parts of Europe also targeted with hoax bomb alerts, among them flights that departed from Dublin. The Irish authorities will mount their largest ever security operation next week when more that 50 prime ministers will visit Dublin for the European Political Community summit on Thursday. That is followed the next day by an informal meeting of the EU Council. The events are being held in the Irish capital as part of Ireland’s six-month presidency of the EU Council. National broadcaster RTÉ was among the media organisations targeted with a threatening email on Friday morning – prompting a security alert that led to the evacuation of its TV and radio studios and offices in Dublin and programmes going off air for a period. With staff allowed to return later in the day, and full broadcasting resuming, Mr Martin appeared on RTÉ One’s flagship Late Late Show on Friday night to speak about the incidents. Taoiseach Micheál Martin (PA). He was asked whether he remained confident that the huge security operation being mounted for the European summits could guarantee their safety. “We’re confident that will go off safely,” he said. “I would say it’s the largest ever security operation in the history of the state. It would be larger than the visit of a US president, for example. Over 50 prime ministers for the European Political Community meeting.” He added: “So combined (the EPC meeting and the informal EU summit), it’s a huge security operation, and huge preparation has gone into this by the Garda, by the Defence Forces, by the Cyber Security Centre and so on.” The Taoiseach said it was too early to say whether there is a Russian connection to the bomb hoaxes that were sent to media outlets. But Mr Martin said the increase in hybrid attacks witnessed across Europe in recent times are undoubtedly linked to Russia. “We can’t be too specific about today yet in terms of who’s responsible,” the Fianna Fáil leader said. He added: “As far back as the Russian invasion of Ukraine, since then the European continent has changed. The level of what we call hybrid attacks, the volume of those attacks have increased exponentially, and the bulk of those were felt in the eastern part of Europe, in the Baltics, in Poland.” Mr Martin continued: “There’s a general view that all of the increases in hybrid attacks has a Russian connection to it. I just can’t say that specifically today in respect of what happened to RTÉ, that’s my point.” The Taoiseach said the hoaxes to media outlets and airlines and the hacking of supermarket refrigeration systems this week were all co-ordinated. RTÉ presenter David McCullagh’s show was affected (Brian Lawless/PA) As well as RTÉ, threats were also sent to Virgin Media, Newstalk and the Irish Independent, Gardaí were called to the scene at RTÉ’s Donnybrook campus in south Dublin on Friday morning. Sniffer dogs were used in searches of the area, which was later declared safe. RTÉ Radio One went off air around 9am on Friday and replaced its programme Today With David McCullagh with a pre-recorded programme of music. The show returned later in the morning, with McCullagh presenting from a mobile broadcasting truck in the car park as gardaí continued to search the RTÉ buildings. Staff including radio and television presenters at the Montrose campus were told to leave the studio buildings after the email was received. Children being looked after in a creche on site were also evacuated. RTÉ director-general Kevin Bakhurst joined staff members outside the station’s mobile broadcast vehicle as they awaited updates of the search. “On the basis of the information we had, we decided that we wanted to put the safety of the staff first and evacuate the buildings,” he said. “It’s a disgraceful attack on the media, on free media, and unfortunately, probably where it comes from, they don’t really appreciate the importance of free media.” McCullagh told listeners the threat warned of a bomb which would explode within 45 minutes. RTÉ presenter Sarah McInerney said the sender of the email claimed to have been part of a group responsible for other recent threats against airlines, and had claimed an operative had planted an explosive device in the building. RTÉ presenter Sarah McInerney speaking outside the RTÉ headquarters in Dublin (Cate McCurry/PA) Ireland’s Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan said the threats were being taken “very seriously” and are being investigated by gardaí. “Europe has increasingly become the target of different forms of hybrid attacks, which are evolving in complexity and sophistication,” he said in a statement. “To counter these threats, it is important to strengthen our co-operation and co-ordination. “Threats of this nature are completely unacceptable and every effort will be made to identify those responsible.” A Garda work-to-rule action for the duration of next week’s high profile events has been directed by a representative organisation for rank-and-file members, while public sector workers are planning a nationwide strike on Thursday. RTÉ continued to broadcast from mobile broadcast vehicles while staff remained evacuated (Cate McCurry/PA) Tánaiste Simon Harris said the Government is “alive” to the risks associated with the types of threats received by Irish media outlets on Friday. “I do want to assure the people of this country is that this is an issue being taken very seriously by the gardaí, by our security forces and our cyber experts,” he told Cork 96FM. “They’re working now on this issue and of course they’ll be liaising as appropriate with European counterparts as well. “The priority is that people are safe, but we need to work to identify the culprits as well. “I want people to know that we’re alive to these risks.” Seamus Dooley, the secretary of the National Union of Journalists in Ireland, said the threat was a “deeply disturbing” attack on press freedom. A Garda spokesperson said: “An Garda Síochána is aware of a threat made against media organisations here and in Europe. “An Garda Síochána has been liaising with the Irish media organisations and the threats will be investigated.” Share Get involved with the news Send your news & photos Loading...
